docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:9:We're building a centralized service to capture webhook events from the various third-party services we use. The first integration will be **Brevo transactional email events**. The architecture will be event-driven and built to scale to additional providers (Stripe, GitHub, etc.) without significant rework.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:27:- Alert dedup/cooldown infrastructure — Sentry's grouping is enough until proven otherwise
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:34:                                                Sentry (error tracking)
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:50:Consumes from `webhooks-queue`. For Brevo transactional email events, writes to the D1 `brevo_email_events` table. On failure: report to Sentry **from inside the consumer** (this is where the stack trace exists — the DLQ handler can't get it later) with the full payload attached, and either throw or call `msg.retry()` to let the queue retry. Acknowledge successfully captured messages with `msg.ack()`.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:53:Receives messages that failed 3 delivery attempts. Retention: configured to 14 days (queue max — default is 4 days, must be explicitly bumped via `wrangler queues update`).
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:56:Consumes from `webhooks-dlq` and writes one row to `webhooks_dlq_audit` so the payload is replayable after the queue's 14-day retention expires. That's it — no alerting, no error context, no dedup logic. The error story is in Sentry (logged from the consumer), the replay payload is in D1.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:80:Intentionally minimal. The audit row exists so we can replay the original payload after the DLQ's 14-day retention expires. Error context lives in Sentry.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:110:- **Sentry** holds the error story. The consumer catches errors and reports to Sentry with the full payload as context, tagged `handler: webhooks-consumer`. The DLQ handler also reports to Sentry (tagged `handler: webhooks-dlq`) only if its own audit insert fails — so a silent DLQ-handler failure doesn't hide. Sentry's own grouping handles "same error, many occurrences" — we don't need our own dedup layer.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:113:No email alerts in v1 — Sentry alert rules cover notification, and routing a Brevo-failure alert through Brevo is a circular dependency we don't want.
docs/development/prd/email-webhook-listener/email-webhook-listener-prd.md:138:- Whether to add a Sentry alert rule day-1 or rely on the dashboard until we see real failures.

docs/development/adr/0001-better-auth-reuses-supabase-user-ids.md:1:# better-auth reuses Supabase user ids during migration
docs/development/adr/0001-better-auth-reuses-supabase-user-ids.md:3:Coffitivity product data is already keyed by the Supabase user id across Supabase tables and D1 app-data tables. During the Supabase to better-auth migration, `auth-api` will create new better-auth users with the matching Supabase user id when an existing Supabase account can be found by email; otherwise better-auth may generate a new id. The Supabase lookup must be isolated as a removable migration adapter so it can be deleted after all users and apps have moved to better-auth.

docs/development/adr/0004-keep-user-api-routes-while-swapping-authentication.md:3:The Supabase to better-auth migration will keep existing `user-api` route paths unless an endpoint's request or response contract changes. Authentication changes should be centralized behind a helper or middleware that first validates better-auth tokens through `auth-api` and temporarily falls back to Supabase JWT validation. Any remaining Supabase-specific code must be isolated and clearly marked as migration-only so it can be found and removed after all clients and services use better-auth.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:13:The provider change must not alter the service-binding contracts used by calling applications or create automatic failover behavior. When the active provider cannot complete a send request, the service must retry twice immediately, report the final failure to Coffitivity's existing Sentry error-monitoring system, and return that failure to its caller. Justin will use the resulting Sentry reports to evaluate the incident and decide whether to switch all transactional sends to Cloudflare.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:23:The service will make at most three requests through the selected provider per message: the initial request and two immediate retries with no delay or backoff. Each SES request has a three-second timeout. After the third failure, the same provider-neutral error returned to the caller is captured once in a dedicated `email-rpc-service` Sentry project without recipient addresses, email content, verification tokens, or OTP values. Sentry notification rules are configured outside the application by Justin.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:25:Production rollout will be staged. The new code will first be deployed while production remains explicitly configured for Cloudflare. SES and Sentry behavior will be exercised in staging, the Cloudflare path will be regression-tested, and production will then be changed to `AWS_SES` in a separate configuration deployment. Cloudflare remains ready for the reverse configuration change if manual rollback is required.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:37:9. As an `email-rpc-service` maintainer, I want all current transactional email methods to share one active provider, so that incident response is predictable.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:45:17. As an operator, I want final SES send failures visible in Sentry after both retries, so that I can assess the volume and type of failure before switching providers.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:46:18. As an operator, I want final Cloudflare send failures visible in Sentry while it is active, so that the backup path cannot fail silently.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:47:19. As an operator, I want Sentry to group and notify on failures according to its external project settings, so that application code does not implement a second alerting system.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:48:20. As an operator, I want a dedicated Sentry project for the email service, so that provider incidents have clear ownership and grouping.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:50:22. As a Coffitivity User, I want recipient addresses, OTP values, tokens, links, subjects, and message bodies excluded from Sentry, so that monitoring does not expose email secrets or personal content.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:51:23. As an operator, I want every final provider-send failure visible in Sentry, so that I can debug the returned error and decide whether its volume indicates an outage.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:75:- Missing provider configuration resolves to `AWS_SES`. Any present but unsupported value produces a non-retryable configuration failure, is reported through Sentry when configured, and is returned to the caller.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:94:- A dedicated `email-rpc-service` Sentry project receives the final failure from either active provider when its DSN is configured.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:95:- Sentry captures the same provider-neutral delivery error returned to the caller and tags the provider, reason, environment, template, status, and provider request or error code when available. AWS events also include a redacted, length-limited copy of the provider's diagnostic message for debugging without changing the generic caller-facing error.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:98:- Sentry reporting is bounded and best-effort. A monitoring failure must not replace or hide the original delivery failure.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:99:- Application code sends no outage-notification email. Justin owns Sentry project and notification-rule configuration outside the repository.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:100:- Only the initial provider request path produces these Sentry reports. SES delivery, bounce, complaint, delay, open, and click webhooks do not generate outage alerts as part of this project.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:103:- Rollout is staged: deploy the implementation while production remains on Cloudflare, validate SES and Sentry in staging, regression-test Cloudflare, cut production over through configuration, then perform a production smoke test.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:104:- The production cutover must verify that SES production sending access, sending quota, the IAM policy, Worker secrets, sender identity, dedicated Sentry project, and Cloudflare backup binding are ready.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:112:- The highest-value seam is the current central delivery orchestration function. Provider-defaulting, explicit selection, invalid configuration, global routing, safe logging, Sentry reporting, and error propagation should be proven there so every RPC method receives the same behavior.
docs/development/prd/aws-ses-primary-email-provider/aws-ses-primary-email-provider-spec.md:119:- Sentry tests prove that reporting occurs only after the active provider reaches a terminal system failure, not before a retry that later succeeds.

docs/development/adr/0008-first-party-attribution-ledger-in-d1.md:3:Attribution Events are recorded in an immutable measurement ledger in app-data D1 rather than in PostHog, which is already installed in `apps/www` and would have supplied funnel reporting for free. The deciding factor is that the next consumer is a CAC tool, which is fundamentally a join across ad spend, Attribution Touches, and Stripe revenue: in D1 that is one SQL statement over data we own, while in PostHog it is an export plus permanent manual reconciliation against Stripe. Three secondary reasons reinforced it — PostHog here is client-side only, so the trial, payment, and subscription-ended events originate in a Worker webhook and are new instrumentation either way; a first-party write to `user-api` avoids the ad-blocker sampling that would silently bias a revenue number; and Cloudflare is already a sub-processor, so the ledger adds no new third party holding personal data. Two consequences a future reader should not mistake for oversights: measurement facts are append-only with no unique constraints, so first-touch versus last-touch and "first payment" versus renewals stay read-time questions rather than being baked into writes; account deletion anonymizes the affected rows by clearing their user, visitor, and Stripe links while retaining aggregate facts; and nothing reads the ledger yet because reporting is a later build that should be designed against real data.

docs/development/adr/0002-auth-api-owns-authentication-for-clients-and-workers.md:3:`auth-api` is the authentication boundary for Coffitivity web clients, future hybrid mobile clients, and backend workers that need to verify user identity. Other workers must not reimplement better-auth session validation or read the auth database directly; they should call a narrow RPC surface exposed by `auth-api` over Cloudflare service bindings, following the same public-types-module pattern used by `email-rpc-service`. The RPC surface should return structured authentication results rather than forcing callers to infer whether a request failed because the user is unauthenticated or because the auth service is unhealthy. During migration, `user-api` may keep a removable Supabase fallback, but better-auth validation belongs in `auth-api`.

docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:8:Supabase JWTs expire after 1 hour. The Supabase JS client auto-refreshes tokens on a timer, but browsers throttle/suspend timers in background tabs. Coffitivity users commonly listen for extended sessions, often with the tab backgrounded. When the auto-refresh timer is suppressed, the stored access token expires silently.
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:10:Current infrastructure services (`ListeningTrackingService`, `RewardsService`, `AudioRepository`) receive the access token as a string parameter captured at call time. If the token was read from the Zustand store after it went stale, every subsequent API call fails with a 401. There is no retry logic — the service throws immediately and Sentry captures the error.
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:12:**Observed Sentry error:** `Error: Unauthorized. at <anonymous> (ListeningTrackingService.ts:96:11)`
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:25:1. **Resolves tokens lazily** — calls `supabase.auth.getSession()` to get the freshest available token right before each request, instead of relying on a previously captured string.
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:26:2. **Caches tokens locally** — reads the JWT `exp` claim to avoid calling Supabase on every API request. Only re-fetches when the token is within 2 minutes of expiry.
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:27:3. **Retries on 401** — on an `Unauthorized` response, explicitly calls `supabase.auth.refreshSession()` and retries the request once with the new token.
docs/development/prd/authenticated-fetch/authenticated-fetch.md:39:Lives in `__shared__/` alongside the Supabase client singleton — it's a cross-layer building block consumed by infrastructure modules.

docs/development/adr/0005-user-api-owns-product-entitlements.md:3:Product Plans are app data, not authentication data. After the Supabase migration, `user-api` will own Plan storage and access decisions in app-data D1, while `auth-api` remains responsible only for authentication. docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:1:# PRD: Supabase → better-auth Migration — Phase 1 (Login & Logout via Email OTP)
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:9:The `www` app currently delegates all authentication to Supabase via `supabase.auth.*` calls wrapped in a static `AuthManager` (`apps/www/src/lib/application/AuthManager.ts`). The Supabase `Session` flows into `appStore.session` and is consumed across ~20 files for user identity, auth-gated UI, and access tokens for `user-api` calls. We're moving off Supabase entirely — the first step is auth.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:15:1. The existing Supabase `AuthManager` is deeply wired into `AppManager`, `appStore`, `ApiClient`, `UserProfileRepository`, and every route that reads `session.user`. A big-bang swap is high risk.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:16:2. Supabase isn't only used for auth — `appStore.setSession` reads `user_meta_data.subscription` directly from Supabase Postgres, and `UserProfileRepository` queries Supabase tables. Those subsystems will get their own migration PRDs later.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:17:3. We need to validate the better-auth flow against real users (cookies, CORS, OTP delivery, session shape) before committing the cutover.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:21:Introduce a **parallel, additive** set of better-auth tools alongside the existing Supabase code so we can exercise the new login/logout flow end-to-end without touching `AuthManager` or `appStore.session`. After this phase, both auth systems can be active simultaneously: existing users continue to authenticate via Supabase; opted-in users can hit the new OTP flow and observe a working better-auth session in app state.

Without it, the better-auth handler will reject cross-origin requests from the www app and the browser will not accept the session cookie. Add explicit config:

docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:146:Mirrors the pattern of `lib/__shared__/supabase/client.ts` so both clients coexist as singletons under `__shared__/`.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:177:- `appStore.session` is typed `Session | null` from `@supabase/supabase-js`. Reusing it would force a type union that ripples into every consumer.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:178:- Subscription state (`isUserSubscribed`, `subscription`) is tightly coupled to the Supabase user via `setSession`'s Postgres query. Keeping the two auth systems in separate stores prevents that coupling from accidentally leaking into the new path.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:185:A class (following the newer `PaymentManager` / `ListeningTrackingService` pattern, not the static-object style of `AuthManager`). Constructor takes the auth client and the store; methods are scoped to v1 only.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:210:- **`initialize()`** — Calls `client.getSession()` once on app boot. If a session is returned (cookie still valid), populate `betterAuthStore.session`. Subscribes to `client`'s session change events if available (`useSession` hook backs the React-friendly path; for the manager layer we just refetch on focus/visibility — see "Out of scope" for the proactive refresh listener). Sets `isAuthLoading` appropriately.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:212:- **`verifyLoginOtp(email, otp)`** — Calls `client.signIn.emailOtp({ email, otp })`. On success, the auth-api sets the session cookie; the manager then fetches the resolved session via `client.getSession()` and writes it to the store. Returns void on success, throws on failure.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:213:- **`signOut()`** — Calls `client.signOut()`, clears `betterAuthStore.session`. Does **not** touch `appStore.session`, the `queryClient`, or any other Supabase state.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:276:- A user can be logged into Supabase (existing flow) and **also** logged into better-auth (new flow) at the same time. The app behavior is determined by `appStore.session` — Supabase wins for everything except the new debug routes.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:277:- A user can be logged out of Supabase but still have a better-auth session, or vice versa. Each store reflects only its own system's truth.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:305:9. Verify existing `/auth/log-in` still works against Supabase. No regression.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:307:#### Cookie / CORS sanity
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:309:The auth-api runs on a different origin (`localhost:8888`) from the www app (`localhost:5173`). The better-auth client must send `credentials: "include"` and the auth-api must respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and an explicit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173` (not `*`). Verify this works end-to-end before assuming the session cookie round-trips correctly. If it doesn't, the auth-api needs either a CORS middleware addition or a `trustedOrigins` config update.
docs/development/prd/supabase-to-better-auth-migration/supabase-to-better-auth-migration.md:314:- **Refresh on visibility / focus** — Supabase auto-refreshes silently. better-auth sessions are cookie-based with an `expiresAt`; for v1 we accept that a stale tab may discover its session is gone on the next request. A visibility listener that calls `client.getSession()` on tab re-focus is a good follow-up (parallels the deferred work in the `authenticated-fetch` PRD).

docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:9:Favorite Tracks are still read and written directly from the web app through Supabase profile data. This keeps Supabase product-data access embedded in the frontend and makes the later Supabase to better-auth cutover larger than it needs to be. The product should first move Favorite Track ownership behind Coffitivity APIs, while leaving request authentication on the current Supabase token path until the auth migration is ready.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:11:Today a Coffitivity User's Favorite Tracks live as an array in legacy profile data. That shape makes Favorite Track updates a frontend read-modify-write operation, relies on browser-side Supabase authorization, and stores app-owned listening preferences outside the app-data D1 store that already owns newer product data such as custom blends, listening sessions, and rewards.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:15:Move Favorite Tracks into `user-api` as app-owned data backed by app-data D1. The web app will call `user-api` for Favorite Track reads and writes, and `user-api` will continue to authenticate those requests with the existing Supabase JWT validation during this first slice. This deliberately reduces the frontend Supabase footprint before the later better-auth cutover.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:17:Favorite Tracks will be stored as active rows, one row per Coffitivity User and track id. The API will expose idempotent per-track add and remove commands instead of whole-list replacement. `user-api` will lazily import legacy Favorite Tracks from Supabase profile data the first time it handles a Favorite Track operation for a Coffitivity User, using a small migration-only import sentinel so import completion is tracked independently from whether the user has active Favorite Track rows.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:26:6. As a signed-in Coffitivity User, I want my old Supabase Favorite Tracks to appear after this change, so that migration does not erase my saved listening preferences.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:28:8. As a new Coffitivity User, I want Favorite Tracks stored only in the new app-owned store, so that no new Supabase profile dependency is created.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:37:17. As a frontend developer, I want the web app to stop calling Supabase profile tables for Favorite Tracks, so that the later auth cutover has less product-data work attached to it.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:41:21. As an API maintainer, I want Favorite Track route behavior to use Coffitivity language, so that future code does not inherit provider-specific Supabase terminology.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:42:22. As an API maintainer, I want Favorite Track auth to be isolated behind the same conceptual Authenticated User boundary that future routes will use, so that switching from Supabase JWT validation to better-auth service validation is smaller later.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:48:28. As an operator, I want Supabase profile access for this feature to be named migration-only, so that final cleanup is easy to find.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:55:- This PRD is intentionally scoped to Favorite Tracks only. Entitlements, Stripe customer linkage, better-auth cutover work, and broad Supabase cleanup are handled by other migration efforts.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:56:- The first implementation will keep request authentication on the current Supabase JWT path inside `user-api`. This is deliberate: the goal is to remove direct frontend Supabase product-data access before swapping the authentication provider.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:57:- Favorite Track route logic should consume an Authenticated User concept rather than raw provider-specific session data wherever practical. The initial implementation may validate through Supabase, but the route should be shaped so a later better-auth auth helper can replace that validation with minimal route churn.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:58:- This Authenticated User boundary is net-new. Existing routes (listening, rewards, user) currently re-inline Bearer-token extraction plus `supabase.auth.getUser` in each handler with no shared middleware. To make the boundary pay off, it should be built as reusable middleware that the favorites sub-router consumes, rather than a third inlined copy. Refactoring the existing routes onto it is out of scope; this PRD only introduces the pattern.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:59:- The web app should stop reading and writing Supabase profile data for Favorite Tracks. It should call `user-api` through the existing authenticated API client.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:65:- Favorite Track routes should be implemented as a dedicated sub-router mounted directly at `/user/favorite-tracks`, registered independently of the existing `userRouter` rather than nested inside it. This avoids a routing collision: `userRouter` already defines a greedy `DELETE /:id` (account deletion), which would otherwise swallow a single-segment favorites path. A separate mounted sub-router (matching the existing listening/rewards router pattern) keeps favorites isolated from `/:id` and avoids relying on route registration order.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:81:- Legacy Supabase profile data should be imported lazily the first time `user-api` handles any Favorite Track operation for a Coffitivity User.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:83:- Legacy import must use a small migration-only sentinel that records whether Supabase profile import has completed for a Coffitivity User. Import completion must not be inferred from the presence or absence of active Favorite Track rows.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:87:- If the legacy Supabase profile read fails (network/outage) during a first operation, the request must fail with a server error (500) and must not write the sentinel. The operation does not proceed past the import on a Supabase failure. This deliberately keeps un-imported users' favorites availability coupled to Supabase during the migration window, in exchange for never skipping the import and never marking a user imported with incomplete data. Import retries on the next request.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:91:- Favorite Track updates must not write new data back to Supabase.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:92:- New Coffitivity Users should not need Supabase profile rows for Favorite Tracks.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:93:- Supabase profile access for import should live behind a clearly named migration-only adapter so cleanup is searchable.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:100:- The frontend `UserProfileRepository` and its Supabase `user_profiles` access (including the lazy `createNewProfileData` profile-row creation) should be removed as part of this PRD. Favorite Tracks is its only consumer, so once www reads and writes Favorite Tracks through `user-api`, the repository and its DI wiring become dead Supabase code. Confirm there is no other caller before deleting.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:109:1. **Import + Supabase read failure** — A first operation whose legacy Supabase read fails returns 500 and does not write the sentinel. The import is never skipped; it retries on the next request. Accepts coupling un-imported users' availability to Supabase during the migration window.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:114:6. **UserProfileRepository** — Removed in this PRD, along with its Supabase `user_profiles` access and DI wiring, after confirming favorites is its only caller.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:127:- Legacy import tests should cover the Supabase lookup error case explicitly: the request fails with a 500 and the sentinel is not written, so a later request retries the import.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:133:- Existing listening and rewards route tests are prior art for route-level Supabase-token authentication and request setup.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:140:- Moving Entitlements out of Supabase.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:141:- Moving Stripe customer linkage out of Supabase.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:144:- Removing Supabase authentication fallback from `user-api`.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:145:- Removing all frontend Supabase usage unrelated to Favorite Tracks.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:146:- Removing all backend Supabase usage.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:156:- This PRD replaces the Favorite Tracks portion of the larger Product Data off Supabase PRD with a smaller implementation target.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:157:- The reason to do this before the better-auth cutover is to make the later auth swap smaller: the frontend should no longer need a Supabase session to authorize Favorite Track product-data access.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:158:- The later better-auth work should be able to replace Supabase JWT validation behind the Authenticated User boundary without changing the public Favorite Track API contract.
docs/development/prd/favorite-tracks-user-api/favorite-tracks-user-api-prd.md:159:- The migration cleanup should be intentionally searchable. Names that include `migration-only`, `legacy`, `Supabase profile`, and `Favorite Track import` are preferred over vague comments.

;\u62DFarr\u0100;p\u1B7F\u1B80\u61B6;\u693D\u0300;bcdos\u1B8F\u1B90\u1B96\u1BA1\u1BA5\u1BA8\u622Arcap;\u6A48\u0100au\u1B9B\u1B9Ep;\u6A46p;\u6A4Aot;\u628Dr;\u6A45;\uC000\u222A\uFE00\u0200alrv\u1BB5\u1BBF\u1BDE\u1BE3rr\u0100;m\u1BBC\u1BBD\u61B7;\u693Cy\u0180evw\u1BC7\u1BD4\u1BD8q\u0270\u1BCE\0\0\u1BD2re\xE3\u1B73u\xE3\u1B75ee;\u62CEedge;\u62CFen\u803B\xA4\u40A4earrow\u0100lr\u1BEE\u1BF3eft\xBB\u1B80ight\xBB\u1BBDe\xE4\u1BDD\u0100ci\u1C01\u1C07onin\xF4\u01F7nt;\u6231lcty;\u632D\u0980AHabcdefhijlorstuwz\u1C38\u1C3B\u1C3F\u1C5D\u1C69\u1C75\u1C8A\u1C9E\u1CAC\u1CB7\u1CFB\u1CFF\u1D0D\u1D7B\u1D91\u1DAB\u1DBB\u1DC6\u1DCDr\xF2\u0381ar;\u6965\u0200glrs\u1C48\u1C4D\u1C52\u1C54ger;\u6020eth;\u6138\xF2\u1133h\u0100;v\u1C5A\u1C5B\u6010\xBB\u090A\u016B\u1C61\u1C67arow;\u690Fa\xE3\u0315\u0100ay\u1C6E\u1C73ron;\u410F;\u4434\u0180;ao\u0332\u1C7C\u1C84\u0100gr\u02BF\u1C81r;\u61CAtseq;\u6A77\u0180glm\u1C91\u1C94\u1C98\u803B\xB0\u40B0ta;\u43B4ptyv;\u69B1\u0100ir\u1CA3\u1CA8sht;\u697F;\uC000\u{1D521}ar\u0100lr\u1CB3\u1CB5\xBB\u08DC\xBB\u101E\u0280aegsv\u1CC2\u0378\u1CD6\u1CDC\u1CE0m\u0180;os\u0326\u1CCA\u1CD4nd\u0100;s\u0326\u1CD1uit;\u6666amma;\u43DDin;\u62F2\u0180;io\u1CE7\u1CE8\u1CF8\u40F7de\u8100\xF7;o\u1CE7\u1CF0ntimes;\u62C7n\xF8\u1CF7cy;\u4452c\u026F\u1D06\0\0\u1D0Arn;\u631Eop;\u630D\u0280lptuw\u1D18\u1D1D\u1D22\u1D49\u1D55lar;\u4024f;\uC000\u{1D555}\u0280;emps\u030B\u1D2D\u1D37\u1D3D\u1D42q\u0100;d\u0352\u1D33ot;\u6251inus;\u6238lus;\u6214quare;\u62A1blebarwedg\xE5\xFAn\u0180adh\u112E\u1D5D\u1D67ownarrow\xF3\u1C83arpoon\u0100lr\u1D72\u1D76ef\xF4\u1CB4igh\xF4\u1CB6\u0162\u1D7F\u1D85karo\xF7\u0F42\u026F\u1D8A\0\0\u1D8Ern;\u631Fop;\u630C\u0180cot\u1D98\u1DA3\u1DA6\u0100ry\u1D9D\u1DA1;\uC000\u{1D4B9};\u4455l;\u69F6rok;\u4111\u0100dr\u1DB0\u1DB4ot;\u62F1i\u0100;f\u1DBA\u1816\u65BF\u0100ah\u1DC0\u1DC3r\xF2\u0429a\xF2\u0FA6angle;\u69A6\u0100ci\u1DD2\u1DD5y;\u445Fgrarr;\u67FF\u0900Dacdefglmnopqrstux\u1E01\u1E09\u1E19\u1E38\u0578\u1E3C\u1E49\u1E61\u1E7E\u1EA5\u1EAF\u1EBD\u1EE1\u1F2A\u1F37\u1F44\u1F4E\u1F5A\u0100Do\u1E06\u1D34o\xF4\u1C89\u0100cs\u1E0E\u1E14ute\u803B\xE9\u40E9ter;\u6A6E\u0200aioy\u1E22\u1E27\u1E31\u1E36ron;\u411Br\u0100;c\u1E2D\u1E2E\u6256\u803B\xEA\u40EAlon;\u6255;\u444Dot;\u4117\u0100Dr\u1E41\u1E45ot;\u6252;\uC000\u{1D522}\u0180;rs\u1E50\u1E51\u1E57\u6A9Aave\u803B\xE8\u40E8\u0100;d\u1E5C\u1E5D\u6A96ot;\u6A98\u0200;ils\u1E6A\u1E6B\u1E72\u1E74\u6A99nters;\u63E7;\u6113\u0100;d\u1E79\u1E7A\u6A95ot;\u6A97\u0180aps\u1E85\u1E89\u1E97cr;\u4113ty\u0180;sv\u1E92\u1E93\u1E95\u6205et\xBB\u1E93p\u01001;\u1E9D\u1EA4\u0133\u1EA1\u1EA3;\u6004;\u6005\u6003\u0100gs\u1EAA\u1EAC;\u414Bp;\u6002\u0100gp\u1EB4\u1EB8on;\u4119f;\uC000\u{1D556}\u0180als\u1EC4\u1ECE\u1ED2r\u0100;s\u1ECA\u1ECB\u62D5l;\u69E3us;\u6A71i\u0180;lv\u1EDA\u1EDB\u1EDF\u43B5on\xBB\u1EDB;\u43F5\u0200csuv\u1EEA\u1EF3\u1F0B\u1F23\u0100io\u1EEF\u1E31rc\xBB\u1E2E\u0269\u1EF9\0\0\u1EFB\xED\u0548ant\u0100gl\u1F02\u1F06tr\xBB\u1E5Dess\xBB\u1E7A\u0180aei\u1F12\u1F16\u1F1Als;\u403Dst;\u625Fv\u0100;D\u0235\u1F20D;\u6A78parsl;\u69E5\u0100Da\u1F2F\u1F33ot;\u6253rr;\u6971\u0180cdi\u1F3E\u1F41\u1EF8r;\u612Fo\xF4\u0352\u0100ah\u1F49\u1F4B;\u43B7\u803B\xF0\u40F0\u0100mr\u1F53\u1F57l\u803B\xEB\u40EBo;\u60AC\u0180cip\u1F61\u1F64\u1F67l;\u4021s\xF4\u056E\u0100eo\u1F6C\u1F74ctatio\xEE\u0559nential\xE5\u0579\u09E1\u1F92\0\u1F9E\0\u1FA1\u1FA7\0\0\u1FC6\u1FCC\0\u1FD3\0\u1FE6\u1FEA\u2000\0\u2008\u205Allingdotse\xF1\u1E44y;\u4444male;\u6640\u0180ilr\u1FAD\u1FB3\u1FC1lig;\u8000\uFB03\u0269\u1FB9\0\0\u1FBDg;\u8000\uFB00ig;\u8000\uFB04;\uC000\u{1D523}lig;\u8000\uFB01lig;\uC000fj\u0180alt\u1FD9\u1FDC\u1FE1t;\u666Dig;\u8000\uFB02ns;\u65B1of;\u4192\u01F0\u1FEE\0\u1FF3f;\uC000\u{1D557}\u0100ak\u05BF\u1FF7\u0100;v\u1FFC\u1FFD\u62D4;\u6AD9artint;\u6A0D\u0100ao\u200C\u2055\u0100cs\u2011\u2052\u03B1\u201A\u2030\u2038\u2045\u2048\0\u2050\u03B2\u2022\u2025\u2027\u202A\u202C\0\u202E\u803B\xBD\u40BD;\u6153\u803B\xBC\u40BC;\u6155;\u6159;\u615B\u01B3\u2034\0\u2036;\u6154;\u6156\u02B4\u203E\u2041\0\0\u2043\u803B\xBE\u40BE;\u6157;\ ;\u62DFarr\u0100;p\u1B7F\u1B80\u61B6;\u693D\u0300;bcdos\u1B8F\u1B90\u1B96\u1BA1\u1BA5\u1BA8\u622Arcap;\u6A48\u0100au\u1B9B\u1B9Ep;\u6A46p;\u6A4Aot;\u628Dr;\u6A45;\uC000\u222A\uFE00\u0200alrv\u1BB5\u1BBF\u1BDE\u1BE3rr\u0100;m\u1BBC\u1BBD\u61B7;\u693Cy\u0180evw\u1BC7\u1BD4\u1BD8q\u0270\u1BCE\0\0\u1BD2re\xE3\u1B73u\xE3\u1B75ee;\u62CEedge;\u62CFen\u803B\xA4\u40A4earrow\u0100lr\u1BEE\u1BF3eft\xBB\u1B80ight\xBB\u1BBDe\xE4\u1BDD\u0100ci\u1C01\u1C07onin\xF4\u01F7nt;\u6231lcty;\u632D\u0980AHabcdefhijlorstuwz\u1C38\u1C3B\u1C3F\u1C5D\u1C69\u1C75\u1C8A\u1C9E\u1CAC\u1CB7\u1CFB\u1CFF\u1D0D\u1D7B\u1D91\u1DAB\u1DBB\u1DC6\u1DCDr\xF2\u0381ar;\u6965\u0200glrs\u1C48\u1C4D\u1C52\u1C54ger;\u6020eth;\u6138\xF2\u1133h\u0100;v\u1C5A\u1C5B\u6010\xBB\u090A\u016B\u1C61\u1C67arow;\u690Fa\xE3\u0315\u0100ay\u1C6E\u1C73ron;\u410F;\u4434\u0180;ao\u0332\u1C7C\u1C84\u0100gr\u02BF\u1C81r;\u61CAtseq;\u6A77\u0180glm\u1C91\u1C94\u1C98\u803B\xB0\u40B0ta;\u43B4ptyv;\u69B1\u0100ir\u1CA3\u1CA8sht;\u697F;\uC000\u{1D521}ar\u0100lr\u1CB3\u1CB5\xBB\u08DC\xBB\u101E\u0280aegsv\u1CC2\u0378\u1CD6\u1CDC\u1CE0m\u0180;os\u0326\u1CCA\u1CD4nd\u0100;s\u0326\u1CD1uit;\u6666amma;\u43DDin;\u62F2\u0180;io\u1CE7\u1CE8\u1CF8\u40F7de\u8100\xF7;o\u1CE7\u1CF0ntimes;\u62C7n\xF8\u1CF7cy;\u4452c\u026F\u1D06\0\0\u1D0Arn;\u631Eop;\u630D\u0280lptuw\u1D18\u1D1D\u1D22\u1D49\u1D55lar;\u4024f;\uC000\u{1D555}\u0280;emps\u030B\u1D2D\u1D37\u1D3D\u1D42q\u0100;d\u0352\u1D33ot;\u6251inus;\u6238lus;\u6214quare;\u62A1blebarwedg\xE5\xFAn\u0180adh\u112E\u1D5D\u1D67ownarrow\xF3\u1C83arpoon\u0100lr\u1D72\u1D76ef\xF4\u1CB4igh\xF4\u1CB6\u0162\u1D7F\u1D85karo\xF7\u0F42\u026F\u1D8A\0\0\u1D8Ern;\u631Fop;\u630C\u0180cot\u1D98\u1DA3\u1DA6\u0100ry\u1D9D\u1DA1;\uC000\u{1D4B9};\u4455l;\u69F6rok;\u4111\u0100dr\u1DB0\u1DB4ot;\u62F1i\u0100;f\u1DBA\u1816\u65BF\u0100ah\u1DC0\u1DC3r\xF2\u0429a\xF2\u0FA6angle;\u69A6\u0100ci\u1DD2\u1DD5y;\u445Fgrarr;\u67FF\u0900Dacdefglmnopqrstux\u1E01\u1E09\u1E19\u1E38\u0578\u1E3C\u1E49\u1E61\u1E7E\u1EA5\u1EAF\u1EBD\u1EE1\u1F2A\u1F37\u1F44\u1F4E\u1F5A\u0100Do\u1E06\u1D34o\xF4\u1C89\u0100cs\u1E0E\u1E14ute\u803B\xE9\u40E9ter;\u6A6E\u0200aioy\u1E22\u1E27\u1E31\u1E36ron;\u411Br\u0100;c\u1E2D\u1E2E\u6256\u803B\xEA\u40EAlon;\u6255;\u444Dot;\u4117\u0100Dr\u1E41\u1E45ot;\u6252;\uC000\u{1D522}\u0180;rs\u1E50\u1E51\u1E57\u6A9Aave\u803B\xE8\u40E8\u0100;d\u1E5C\u1E5D\u6A96ot;\u6A98\u0200;ils\u1E6A\u1E6B\u1E72\u1E74\u6A99nters;\u63E7;\u6113\u0100;d\u1E79\u1E7A\u6A95ot;\u6A97\u0180aps\u1E85\u1E89\u1E97cr;\u4113ty\u0180;sv\u1E92\u1E93\u1E95\u6205et\xBB\u1E93p\u01001;\u1E9D\u1EA4\u0133\u1EA1\u1EA3;\u6004;\u6005\u6003\u0100gs\u1EAA\u1EAC;\u414Bp;\u6002\u0100gp\u1EB4\u1EB8on;\u4119f;\uC000\u{1D556}\u0180als\u1EC4\u1ECE\u1ED2r\u0100;s\u1ECA\u1ECB\u62D5l;\u69E3us;\u6A71i\u0180;lv\u1EDA\u1EDB\u1EDF\u43B5on\xBB\u1EDB;\u43F5\u0200csuv\u1EEA\u1EF3\u1F0B\u1F23\u0100io\u1EEF\u1E31rc\xBB\u1E2E\u0269\u1EF9\0\0\u1EFB\xED\u0548ant\u0100gl\u1F02\u1F06tr\xBB\u1E5Dess\xBB\u1E7A\u0180aei\u1F12\u1F16\u1F1Als;\u403Dst;\u625Fv\u0100;D\u0235\u1F20D;\u6A78parsl;\u69E5\u0100Da\u1F2F\u1F33ot;\u6253rr;\u6971\u0180cdi\u1F3E\u1F41\u1EF8r;\u612Fo\xF4\u0352\u0100ah\u1F49\u1F4B;\u43B7\u803B\xF0\u40F0\u0100mr\u1F53\u1F57l\u803B\xEB\u40EBo;\u60AC\u0180cip\u1F61\u1F64\u1F67l;\u4021s\xF4\u056E\u0100eo\u1F6C\u1F74ctatio\xEE\u0559nential\xE5\u0579\u09E1\u1F92\0\u1F9E\0\u1FA1\u1FA7\0\0\u1FC6\u1FCC\0\u1FD3\0\u1FE6\u1FEA\u2000\0\u2008\u205Allingdotse\xF1\u1E44y;\u4444male;\u6640\u0180ilr\u1FAD\u1FB3\u1FC1lig;\u8000\uFB03\u0269\u1FB9\0\0\u1FBDg;\u8000\uFB00ig;\u8000\uFB04;\uC000\u{1D523}lig;\u8000\uFB01lig;\uC000fj\u0180alt\u1FD9\u1FDC\u1FE1t;\u666Dig;\u8000\uFB02ns;\u65B1of;\u4192\u01F0\u1FEE\0\u1FF3f;\uC000\u{1D557}\u0100ak\u05BF\u1FF7\u0100;v\u1FFC\u1FFD\u62D4;\u6AD9artint;\u6A0D\u0100ao\u200C\u2055\u0100cs\u2011\u2052\u03B1\u201A\u2030\u2038\u2045\u2048\0\u2050\u03B2\u2022\u2025\u2027\u202A\u202C\0\u202E\u803B\xBD\u40BD;\u6153\u803B\xBC\u40BC;\u6155;\u6159;\u615B\u01B3\u2034\0\u2036;\u6154;\u6156\u02B4\u203E\u2041\0\0\u2043\u803B\xBE\u40BE;\u6157;\ apps/blog/src/content/editorial/scrapbook/freelance-hacks-tax-tips-for-self-employment/index.md:24:If you’re feeling behind the 8 Ball even with a few extra days, make sure to file an extension for your personal taxes (super easy to do through most tax software). You can also head to the [IRS FreeFile](https://apps.irs.gov/app/freeFile/jsp/index.jsp?ck) page for a run down of options to file your extension for free. Remember, as of 1/1/16, the IRS has the power to revoke or deny your passport in certain cases of unpaid taxes, so use the extra few days to take a look while you still have time!
apps/blog/src/content/editorial/scrapbook/freelance-hacks-tax-tips-for-self-employment/index.md:26:**3) Keep track of your expenses.**
apps/blog/src/content/editorial/scrapbook/freelance-hacks-tax-tips-for-self-employment/index.md:28:If you’re self-employed, you have ample opportunities to take tax deductions. Anything including your home office, mileage driving, meetings, coffees with clients, and the water bottles you keep stocked in your Uber can be written off if you’re prudent about keeping records of these expenditures. Fortunately there are some great options out there for tracking expenses. Check out [QuickBooks Self-Employed](http://quickbooks.intuit.com/self-employed/) or [Xero Tax Touch](https://www.xero.com/us/taxtouch/) for a great way to categorize expenditures for clients. [MileIQ](https://www.mileiq.com/) can help you log mileage and [99Deductions](https://99deductions.com/) can help you understand what you can expense. While you’re at it, take a look at [Hurdlr](https://hurdlr.com/), a holistic finance app for freelancers built by 99Deductions. With so much awesome technology at our fingertips, there’s no reason to get behind on expenses over the year! This will make all the difference in driving down your total end of the year tax obligation.
apps/blog/src/content/editorial/scrapbook/freelance-hacks-tax-tips-for-self-employment/index.md:36:Saving is hard — no surprise here. Even if you’re meticulous about your expenses, you’re still expected to pay quarterly estimated taxes on roughly 30% of your self-employment income, which means you need to be keeping an eye on not only how much you earn, but how much you set aside for Uncle Sam. The good news is we’ve created a solution so that you can focus on your work and we can save your money for you. [Painless1099](https://painless1099.com/home?utm_source=coffitivity%20&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=freelancehacks)  is a smart bank account that automates tax withholding from each payment of 1099 income you receive. With a Painless1099 account, all you have to do is connect your direct deposit or invoicing tool (like [Quickbooks Invoicing](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/invoicing/), [Freshbooks](https://www.freshbooks.com/), or [Harvest](https://www.getharvest.com/)) to your new smart savings account and input a few tidbits of information about your tax status. Once you’re setup, Painless will watch for 1099 income, separate taxes based on your tax status, and pass your spendable cash along to your personal checking account. We get it, you’re busy as a freelancer, which is why we made it easy to be prepare for tax season. All in all, tax season doesn’t have to be stressful. The beauty of staying on top of your 1099 taxes is that you can treat April as if it’s just another month. If you’re ever looking for more tips on being self-employed, you can talk to our team on the chat portal on our [home page](https://painless1099.com/home?utm_source=coffitivity%20&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=freelancehacks). Keep in mind we’re offering free lifetime withholding for our awesome beta users, so go sign up for [Painless1099](https://painless1099.com/home?utm_source=coffitivity%20&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=freelancehacks) today!

apps/blog/src/content/editorial/scrapbook/the-time-to-go-remote-is-now/index.md:47:Working remotely has another benefit: You can choose where you live. Your clients might be in Manhattan or San Francisco, but, if you don't want to be, you don't have to (and you don't have to pay the exorbitant rents there, either). That means you can control your cost of living. When all you need is an internet connection to get your work done, you can live almost anywhere. Check out [this list](http://www.forbes.com/sites/jaymcgregor/2014/08/13/the-cheapest-cities-in-the-world-to-work-remotely/#e26a64c184ce) of the cheapest cities to work remotely in—you might be surprised at how little you need to make to cover your housing costs and basic living expenses in some of the biggest cities in the world.

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

/**
 * Terms Page CMS Integration Tests
 * Verifies that the Terms page correctly loads and renders content from PayloadCMS
 * using the generic page-intro-block and section-block components
 */

test.describe("Terms Page CMS Integration", () => {
    test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
        await page.goto("/terms");
        // Wait for CMS content to load
        await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");
    });

    test("should load and display CMS content", async ({ page }) => {
        // Verify the page title exists (from page-intro-block)
        const h1 = page.locator("h1");
        await expect(h1).toBeVisible();

        const title = await h1.textContent();
        expect(title).toBeTruthy();
        expect(title!.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    });

    test("should render page intro block (page-intro-block)", async ({ page }) => {
        // The page should have an H1 title
        const h1 = page.locator("main h1");
        await expect(h1).toBeVisible();

        // Title should be meaningful
        const titleText = await h1.textContent();
        expect(titleText).toContain("Terms");

        // The intro section should exist (contains H1)
        const introSection = page.locator("main section:has(h1)");
        await expect(introSection).toBeVisible();
    });

    test("should render multiple section blocks", async ({ page }) => {
        // Should have multiple H2 headings (from section-block components)
        const h2Headings = page.locator("h2");
        const h2Count = await h2Headings.count();

        // Terms page should have many sections (at least 10)
        expect(h2Count).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(10);

        // Each H2 should be visible and have content
        for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(h2Count, 3); i++) {
            const heading = h2Headings.nth(i);
            await expect(heading).toBeVisible();

            const headingText = await heading.textContent();
            expect(headingText).toBeTruthy();
            expect(headingText!.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
        }
    });

    test("should render section numbers correctly", async ({ page }) => {
        // Find sections with numbered titles (e.g., "1. TERMS OF USE")
        const numberedHeadings = page.locator('h2:text-matches("[0-9]+\\.")');
        const count = await numberedHeadings.count();

        // Should have at least some numbered sections
        expect(count).toBeGreaterThan(0);

        // First numbered heading should contain "1."
        if (count > 0) {
            const firstNumbered = await numberedHeadings.first().textContent();
            expect(firstNumbered).toMatch(/^1\./);
        }
    });

    test("should have substantial content in sections", async ({ page }) => {
        // Each section should have paragraphs with content
        const sections = page.locator("main section");
        const sectionCount = await sections.count();

        expect(sectionCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

        // Check sections with H2 have meaningful content
        const sectionsWithH2 = page.locator("main section:has(h2)");
        const h2SectionCount = await sectionsWithH2.count();

        for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(h2SectionCount, 3); i++) {
            const section = sectionsWithH2.nth(i);
            const textContent = await section.textContent();

            // Each section should have substantial text (more than just a title)
            expect(textContent!.length).toBeGreaterThan(50);
        }
    });

    test("should respect max-width constraint", async ({ page }) => {
        // The main container should have max-w-[90ch] class for readability
        const mainContainer = page.locator("div.max-w-\\[90ch\\]");
        await expect(mainContainer).toBeVisible();
    });

    test("should have proper semantic HTML structure", async ({ page }) => {
        // Should have proper heading hierarchy
        const h1 = page.locator("main h1");
        const h1Count = await h1.count();
        expect(h1Count).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1); // At least one H1

        // Should have sections with H2 headings
        const sectionsWithH2 = page.locator("main section:has(h2)");
        const sectionCount = await sectionsWithH2.count();
        expect(sectionCount).toBeGreaterThan(5); // Multiple sections

        // First few sections with H2 should have visible H2
        for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(sectionCount, 3); i++) {
            const section = sectionsWithH2.nth(i);
            const h2InSection = section.locator("h2");
            await expect(h2InSection).toBeVisible();
        }
    });

    test("should display formatted rich text content", async ({ page }) => {
        // Should have paragraphs
        const paragraphs = page.locator("p");
        const paragraphCount = await paragraphs.count();
        expect(paragraphCount).toBeGreaterThan(10);

        // At least some paragraphs should have substantial content
        for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(paragraphCount, 5); i++) {
            const p = paragraphs.nth(i);
            const text = await p.textContent();

            if (text && text.length > 20) {
                expect(text.length).toBeGreaterThan(20);
            }
        }
    });

    test("should not show error state", async ({ page }) => {
        // Should not have error messages in main content
        const errorText = page.locator("main >> text=/failed to load|something went wrong/i");
        const errorCount = await errorText.count();
        expect(errorCount).toBe(0);

        // Verify CMS content loaded (has H1 and H2s)
        const h1 = page.locator("main h1");
        await expect(h1).toBeVisible();

        const h2Count = await page.locator("main h2").count();
        expect(h2Count).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    });

    test("should have proper spacing between sections", async ({ page }) => {
        // The main container should have gap-8 for spacing
        const mainContainer = page.locator("div.gap-8");
        await expect(mainContainer).toBeVisible();
    });
});

                <P>
                    Coffitivity believes in limited collection of data. The site currently
                    only collects email addresses as supplied by users during the sign-up
                    process.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>13. PAYMENT DATA COLLECTED</H2>
                <P>
                    Coffitivity relies on a partner payment system through STRIPE to
                    handle and store payment information. No user payment information or
                    data is stored on any Coffitivity owned system or server.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>14. REQUEST FOR REMOVAL</H2>
                <P>
                    If you would like your personal data to be removed from our servers
                    you can delete your account. This process will delete all data that we
                    are not legally required to maintain (like transaction history).
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>15. INFORMATION COLLECTED</H2>
                <P>
                    As a visitor to our site, you can browse our pages without having any
                    personally identifiable information revealed about you. Information we
                    automatically collect via industry standard web log files and other
                    tools includes the URL from which you visited, the page you are
                    visiting, your computer browser information and your IP address. We
                    may also track the effectiveness of various promotions through the use
                    of data collection devices known as "cookies." Cookies contain
                    specific pieces of information on your computer hard drive, and can be
                    set to store information during a visit or for a longer period of
                    time. Our cookies are not tied to personally identifiable information.
                    Third party vendors, including Google, show our ads on sites on the
                    internet. Third party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve
                    ads based on a user's prior visits to our website. Users may opt out
                    of Google's use of cookies by visiting the Google advertising opt-out
                    page.
                </P>
                <P>
                    In addition, there are portions of this web site where we may need to
                    collect personal information from you for a specific purpose, such as
                    to provide you with certain information you request. The information
                    collected from you may include your e-mail address.
                </P>
                <P>
                    This web site is not intended for persons under 13 years of age. We do
                    not knowingly solicit or collect personal information from or about
                    children, and we do not knowingly market our products or services to
                    children.
                </P>
                <P>
                    Except as stated above, we do not share, sell, or lease personal
                    information about you to any third-parties.
                </P>
                <P>
                    It is possible that our business may be merged with or sold to another
                    business entity. During such a transaction, business information is
                    typically one of the assets shared in the combined entity. In the
                    event that this occurs, your personal information will be protected by
                    the Coffitivity privacy policy in effect at the time.
                </P>
                <P>
                    As a good corporate citizen, Coffitivity is interested in protecting
                    the community at large. We will release personal information to legal
                    authorities when we believe it is appropriate to comply with the law.
                    In addition, Coffitivity may choose to release information about you
                    to relevant parties in relation to investigations of fraud, piracy or
                    other unlawful activity.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>16. LINKS TO OTHER SITES</H2>
                <P>
                    Coffitivity's web site may contain links to other sites such as
                    Coffitivity distributors and sales affiliates. While we try to link
                    only to sites that share our high standards and respect for privacy,
                    we are not responsible for the content, security, or privacy practices
                    employed by other sites.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>17. SECURITY OF COLLECTED INFORMATION</H2>
                <P>
                    We maintain strict physical, electronic, and administrative safeguards
                    to protect your personal information from unauthorized or
                    inappropriate access. We restrict access to information about you to
                    those Coffitivity workers who need to know the information to respond
                    to your inquiry or request. Workers who misuse personal information
                    are subject to disciplinary action.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>18. EMAILS</H2>
                <P>
                    Coffitivity may send you emails about your account (access, payments,
                    updates to our services, etc.), including promotional emails. You can
                    opt out of promotional emails at any time by following the
                    instructions in the email.
                </P>
            </section>

            <section>
                <H2>18. CHANGES TO THIS POLICY</H2>
                <P>
                    Please check this privacy policy periodically to inform yourself of
                    any changes. We reserve the right to modify or supplement this privacy
                    policy at any time.
                </P>
                <P>Last updated: January 02, 2026</P>
            </section>
        </div>

From our little home office to wherever you're reading this, we wanted to reflect on a meaningful year and share what's ahead.\n\nWhen we relaunched our little web app in March, we weren't sure how it would be received. We're thrilled and humbled by the kindness, encouragement, and engagement we've received. Your words about how our sounds have helped with focus, writing, studying and more have renewed our sense of direction. Your feedback has guided every change we've made.\n\n## What We Shipped in 2025\n\n- 12 new cafe tracks\n- 50+ additional tracks (Soundscapes, Brain Waves, Sound Colors, etc.)\n- A new interface to showcase our extended library\n- Stability and bug fixes based on your top feedback\n\n## We Listened, You Spoke, We Changed\n\nYour feedback didn't just guide features, it reshaped our approach entirely.\n\nSeveral of you told us that ads on the free tier were distracting, pulling you out of the very focus we're trying to create. You were right. While it certainly improved our bottom line, we realized advertising was antithetical to our [mission](https://coffitivity.com/about). We want you in your best flow state, not constantly thrown out of it. So we've replaced ads with a simple daily time limit on the free tier — no longer ad-supported.\n\nWe also heard loud and clear: many of you don't want additional tracks or features. You just want the original cafe sounds with no disruptions. So we've added a new, more affordable plan that gives you exactly that — just the classics, uninterrupted.\n\nAnd for everyone who asked for a lifetime subscription? Expect it later this month!\n\n## What's Next for 2026?\n\nWe're bringing offline support, task timers, and eventually a relaunch of our mobile apps. We have these initiatives and more documented on [our public roadmap](https://trello.com/b/hOirZSFf/coffitivity-feature-development). We'd love your input on what you want most.\n\n## If you'd like to help\n\n- Submit your thoughts on [features and improvements](https://coffitivity.com/contact).\n- Share us with a friend who might benefit from a relaxed coffee shop vibe.\n\nThank you for being here. Running this project together has been a joy, and the support from this community is what makes it possible.\n\n*Here's to a creative, focused start to 2026,*\n*Justin, Ace, and Ashley*","src/content/editorial/coffitivity-hq/2025-year-in-review/index.md","b740ed5aecd735de",{"html":24,"metadata":25},"\u003Cp>Happy New Year! 2.0: The Biggest Update Since 2015 Is Here!","The biggest Coffitivity update since 2015 — a major library expansion, new ways to engage, and a community-driven roadmap.",["Date","2025-03-09T00:00:00.000Z"],[13],"__ASTRO_IMAGE_./hero.png","https://coffitivity.com/the-buzz/v2-launch",[],[],[],"feature-launch","Coffitivity has always been about bringing the creative energy of a café right to your workspace — wherever that may be. Whether you're working from home, in an office, or on the go, our carefully curated coffee shop soundscapes have helped millions find focus, flow, and inspiration. Now, after years of development, feedback, and support from our incredible community, we're thrilled to introduce **Coffitivity 2.0** — our biggest update since 2015! This new version brings a massive expansion of content, new ways to engage, and a future filled with even more possibilities.\n\n## What's New in Coffitivity 2.0?\n\nWith Coffitivity 2.0, we're giving you more of what you love — diverse, immersive soundscapes designed to inspire creativity and enhance focus. Here's what's in store:\n\n### 44 New Tracks\n\n[![44 New Tracks](44-new-tracks.webp)](https://coffitivity.com/library)\n\nWe're expanding beyond café chatter with sounds that fuel your workflow, and we'll continue growing this collection over time.\n\n### 8 New Cafés\n\n[![8 New Cafés](cafe.webp)](https://coffitivity.com/library/collections/cafes)\n\nExperience the ambiance of even more bustling coffee shops from around the world.\n\n### 16 Soundscapes\n\n[![16 Soundscapes](soundscape.webp)](https://coffitivity.com/library/collections/soundscapes)\n\nFrom cozy cafés to lively urban environments, find the perfect backdrop for your productive moments.\n\n### 9 Brain Waves\n\n[![9 Brain Waves](brain-wave.webp)](https://coffitivity.com/library/collections/brain-waves)\n\nHarness the power of scientifically backed frequencies to help with concentration, relaxation, and creativity.\n\n### 5 Sound Colors\n\n[![5 Sound Colors](sound-color.webp)](https://coffitivity.com/library/collections/sound-colors)\n\nDive into white noise, pink noise, brown noise, and more to create a distraction-free atmosphere that works for you.\n\nBut we're not stopping there. Our roadmap is packed with exciting updates, including **meditation and mindfulness tracks, music integrations, and more ways to tailor your audio environment to your workflow.**\n\n## Looking Ahead: A Community-Driven Future\n\nCoffitivity 2.0 is just the beginning. We believe in building this experience alongside you — our dedicated users. Here are a few ways you can get involved:\n\n- **Help shape the future.** We're sharing our product roadmap publicly so you can see what's coming next. Check our [Trello board](https://trello.com/b/hOirZSFf/coffitivity-feature-development) to help prioritize upcoming features and soundscapes.\n- **Suggest features & soundscapes.** Got an idea for a new feature, café vibe, or productivity tool? Use our [Feature Request form](https://coffitivity.com/contact) to let us know what you'd love to see in Coffitivity.\n\n## A HUGE Thank You\n\nCoffitivity would not be where it is today without our amazing community. Your feedback, suggestions, and passion for this platform have been invaluable in shaping Coffitivity 2.0. Whether you've been with us since the beginning or you're just discovering us now, we appreciate you.\n\nThis update is built for you — and with you. As we continue evolving, we're committed to keeping Coffitivity an inspiring, useful, and community-driven experience.\n\nThank you for your support. Thank you for your ideas. And thank you for letting Coffitivity be a part of your creative journey.\n\nNow, let's get to work — café vibes included. Not as a productivity rule. As a small tool.",["Date","2026-06-25T00:00:00.000Z"],"field-notes",[181,182,183],"sound","creativity","rituals",[185],{"series":186,"slug":187},"science-simplified","is-noise-always-bad",[],[],"10-minute setup, one work session to test","Easy",[193,194,195],"Brainstorming or ideation","Rough drafting","Restarting after a quiet slump","Pick one open-ended task, turn on a moderate café-like soundscape, and work for 20 minutes before deciding whether it helped.","Sometimes silence is exactly wrong for the work in front of you.\n\nNot always, and not even most of the time. But when you're trying to come up with something new and the room feels a little too sharp, a little ambient texture can be the difference between staring at the page and actually moving. There's research behind this. If you want the deeper version, our companion piece, [Is Noise Always Bad for Creative Thinking?](/science-simplified/is-noise-always-bad/), walks through the study. This Field Note is about what to do with the finding in real life.\n\n## When it helps\n\nThe easiest mistake is to treat background buzz like a productivity cheat code. It's more useful to treat it as a tool for a specific kind of work.\n\nReach for it when the task is open-ended: brainstorming, rough drafting, naming, sketching directions, looking for non-obvious connections. Those are the moments when a perfectly silent room can start to feel a little too sharp. The moderate-noise finding is useful here because it gives you permission to stop chasing silence as the default ideal.\n\nThe common thread isn't busyness. It's openness. If the task needs exploration, moderate background buzz may help. If the task needs precision, quiet probably still wins.\n\n## How to dial it in\n\nThe practical word in the study isn't *noise*. It's *moderate*.\n\nIf the sound makes you strain, if it pulls your attention every few seconds, or if you feel the urge to fight it, you're probably past the sweet spot. You want the room to feel inhabited, not loud. Present, not demanding. Something you notice at the start of the session and then mostly stop thinking about.\n\nThat applies whether you're using speakers, headphones, or an actual coffee shop. If headphones make the environment feel too close, lower the volume. If the room still feels dead, raise it a little. The point isn't to imitate someone else's exact setup. The point is to create just enough texture for idea work.\n\nIf you want a ready-made starting point, [Coffitivity](https://coffitivity.com) is a consistent café-like soundscape that saves you the hunt for the right shop, playlist, or rain mix. Pick one, keep the volume moderate, and you've got the same conditions session to session. That repeatability matters for the experiment at the bottom of this page.\n\n## When to skip it\n\nThis is where the study's limits matter most.\n\nDon't force background buzz onto work that clearly wants something else. If you're editing sentence by sentence, proofreading, doing admin, memorizing, or trying to catch small mistakes, quiet is likely better. The same goes for days when you already feel overstimulated. Helpful friction is still friction. If you're running low, even moderate ambience can feel like one demand too many.\n\nThe win isn't becoming a person who always works with sound. The win is learning which tasks benefit from a little atmosphere and which ones don't.\n\n## Try this\n\nFor one work session:\n\n1. Pick one open-ended task that's been hard to start.\n2. Turn on a moderate café-like soundscape.\n3. Work for 20 minutes without changing the setup.\n4. At the end, ask one question: did the task feel easier to enter and stay inside?\n\nIf yes, try it again with similar work. If no, change the volume, change the task type, or go back to quiet. The goal isn't to prove the study in your apartment. The goal is to notice what kind of environment helps you think a little more freely.","src/content/editorial/field-notes/use-background-buzz-when-you-need-ideas/index.md","dfe1a5b0ad74733a",{"html":201,"metadata":202},"\u003Cp>Sometimes silence is exactly wrong for the work in front of you.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Not always, and not even most of the time. If you’re editing sentence by sentence, proofreading, doing admin, memorizing, or trying to catch small mistakes, quiet is likely better. The same goes for days when you already feel overstimulated. Helpful friction is still friction. If you’re running low, even moderate ambience can feel like one demand too many.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>The win isn’t becoming a person who always works with sound. The win is learning which tasks benefit from a little atmosphere and which ones don’t.\u003C/p>\n\u003Ch2 id=\"try-this\">Try this\u003C/h2>\n\u003Cp>For one work session:\u003C/p>\n\u003Col>\n\u003Cli>Pick one open-ended task that’s been hard to start.\u003C/li>\n\u003Cli>Turn on a moderate café-like soundscape.\u003C/li>\n\u003Cli>Work for 20 minutes without changing the setup.\u003C/li>\n\u003Cli>At the end, ask one question: did the task feel easier to enter and stay inside?\u003C/li>\n\u003C/ol>\n\u003Cp>If yes, try it again with similar work. If no, change the volume, change the task type, or go back to quiet. The goal isn’t to prove the study in your apartment. The goal is to notice what kind of environment helps you think a little more freely.\u003C/p>",{"headings":203,"localImagePaths":216,"remoteImagePaths":217,"frontmatter":218,"imagePaths":224},[204,207,210,213],{"depth":28,"slug":205,"text":206},"when-it-helps","When it helps",{"depth":28,"slug":208,"text":209},"how-to-dial-it-in","How to dial it in",{"depth":28,"slug":211,"text":212},"when-to-skip-it","When to skip it",{"depth":28,"slug":214,"text":215},"try-this","Try this",[],[],{"status":6,"title":176,"description":177,"publishedDate":219,"author":10,"series":179,"topics":220,"estimatedTime":190,"difficulty":191,"bestFor":221,"tryThis":196,"relatedEditorial":222},["Date","2026-06-25T00:00:00.000Z"],[181,182,183],[193,194,195],[223],{"series":186,"slug":187},[],"science-simplified/is-noise-always-bad",{"id":225,"data":227,"body":248,"filePath":249,"digest":250,"rendered":251},{"status":6,"title":228,"description":229,"publishedDate":230,"author":10,"series":186,"topics":231,"featured":14,"relatedEditorial":232,"relatedHelp":235,"highlightOn":236,"tldr":237,"sources":238},"Is Noise Always Bad for Creative Thinking?","The 2012 study that convinced us a café-level buzz isn't just pleasant. It might actually help you think.",["Date","2026-06-25T00:00:00.000Z"],[181,182],[233],{"series":179,"slug":234},"use-background-buzz-when-you-need-ideas",[],[],"Too quiet doesn't help creative thinking. Too loud actively hurts it. A moderate buzz, roughly the level of a busy café, came out on top.",[239],{"title":240,"url":241,"publisher":242,"authors":243,"year":247},"Is Noise Always Bad? Exploring the Effects of Ambient Noise on Creative Cognition","/research/Mehta-NoiseAlwaysBad-2012.pdf","Journal of Consumer Research",[244,245,246],"Ravi Mehta","Rui (Juliet) Zhu","Amar Cheema","2012","This is the study that built Coffitivity.\n\nThe one that convinced us a moderate, café-like soundscape was worth making, and the one we still come back to whenever we think about sound and focus. Its question is deceptively simple: is noise always bad for the kind of thinking where you're trying to come up with something new?\n\nThe 2012 *Journal of Consumer Research* paper \u003Ca href=\"/research/Mehta-NoiseAlwaysBad-2012.pdf\">\u003Cem>Is Noise Always Bad? Exploring the Effects of Ambient Noise on Creative Cognition\u003C/em>\u003C/a>, by Ravi Mehta, Rui (Juliet) Zhu, and Amar Cheema, lands on an answer that still surprises most people.\n\n## What they found\n\nThe pattern wasn't a straight line. It was a curve.\n\nAcross five experiments, the researchers compared three noise levels: a quiet 50 decibels, a moderate 70 decibels, and a louder 85 decibels. The moderate level, roughly the buzz of a busy café, produced better creative performance than either the quiet condition or the loud one. The exact numbers matter less than the shape of the result. Quieter wasn't best. Louder wasn't best. The middle won.\n\nAnd the benefit wasn't only about generating odd or unusual ideas. In one experiment, ideas from the moderate-noise condition were rated as both more original *and* more useful. In a final field study, people in noisier (but still moderate) settings showed more interest in genuinely innovative products. That effect was strongest among people who were already creatively inclined.\n\n## How they tested it\n\nThe researchers came at the question from several angles, which is part of why the paper holds up.\n\nFirst, they had people work through creative tasks (word-association puzzles and open-ended idea generation) under each of the three noise levels. Next, they tested *why* the moderate level might be helping. They measured how distracted people felt, how abstractly they were thinking, how long they spent on each task, and even their heart rate and blood pressure. Finally, they left the lab. In a student lounge, they measured real-world ambient noise while asking participants about their interest in innovative products.\n\nThe sound itself wasn't a clean lab tone. The researchers blended cafeteria chatter, roadside traffic, and distant construction into a single track, then adjusted the volume for each condition. The goal was something that felt like real life, not a sterile beep.\n\nMost participants in the controlled experiments were university students, and the paper used a range of creative tasks rather than relying on one. That choice matters: it makes the findings harder to dismiss as a quirk of any single measure.\n\n## Why it might work\n\nThe authors think a moderate buzz creates just enough mental friction (they call it *processing disfluency*) to nudge the brain into a different mode.\n\nThe room isn't quiet enough to feel effortless, but it isn't so loud that thinking falls apart. That low-grade friction, they argue, pushes people toward more abstract thinking. Instead of staying with the most obvious details, you step back. You make broader connections. You think less literally. And that kind of thinking tends to help creative work.\n\nThe loud condition was a different story. At 85 decibels, the noise didn't just distract people a little more; it appeared to reduce how much information they processed at all. Useful friction crossed the line into overload.\n\nThe authors also tested an alternative explanation: maybe moderate noise just makes you more alert, and that's what's helping. Heart rate and blood pressure did rise at first, but the creativity effect held even after that physical alertness wore off. The mental-friction story fit better than the arousal story.\n\n## What this doesn't mean\n\nIt doesn't mean louder is always better. One of the clearest findings in the paper is that the loud condition *hurt* creative performance. There's a ceiling, and crossing it has a cost.\n\nIt also doesn't mean noise helps every kind of thinking. The paper is specific to creative tasks: generating ideas, finding novel solutions. It says nothing about memorizing a list, doing your taxes, or any of the other reasons you might want a quiet room.\n\nAnd it's one paper. Several of its experiments used university students in controlled settings, and the soundtrack was one particular blend. The explanation is carefully argued, but future research could refine or challenge parts of it. Take this as a strong signal, not the last word.\n\n## Why it matters\n\nThe point isn't a magic number. The point is that the effect of sound on your thinking depends on *what kind of thinking you're doing* and *how loud the room is*.\n\nThat matters most for open-ended work: brainstorming, sketching ideas, looking for an angle, trying to solve something the obvious approach hasn't cracked. A perfectly silent room isn't automatically the best setting for that kind of thinking. Sometimes a little ambient texture is exactly what helps you find the unexpected move.\n\nIt's also a good reminder that scientific claims are shaped by their methods. This finding comes from five experiments, several different creative tasks, and one more natural setting. That doesn't make it universal, but it does make it worth taking seriously.\n\nIf you want the practical version of all this, our companion Field Note, [Use Background Buzz When You Need Ideas](/field-notes/use-background-buzz-when-you-need-ideas/), turns the study into a small experiment you can try for yourself.","src/content/editorial/science-simplified/is-noise-always-bad/index.md","6dcb3db70cbea3de",{"html":252,"metadata":253},"\u003Cp>This is the study that built Coffitivity.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>The one that convinced us a moderate, café-like soundscape was worth making, and the one we still come back to whenever we think about sound and focus. Other Productivity Tool You Need\n\nYou sit down to work at the computer. 45 minutes later you realize that you’ve gotten hardly anything done because you’ve been checking email, the news, your social feeds, the latest price on that phone case you want... Sound familiar?\n\nWe’re all living that reality – a constant, vast world of compelling digital distractions that continually demand our attention.\n\nFortunately, there’s a way to eliminate those distractions and even break your habit of succumbing to them. The answer is Freedom.\n\nFreedom gives you complete control over digital distractions, allowing you to block specific websites, apps or the entire internet when and where you want. The [Freedom](https://freedom.sjv.io/XxkaOa) platform works in sync across all your Mac, Windows iOS and Android devices.\n\nHere are some ways to use Freedom and to get your work done without falling into the trap of digital distractions.\n\nBLOCK WEBSITES\n\nWhether meeting a deadline or studying – we’ve all needed a little help staying focused. This is what Freedom is most known for – blocking distracting sites. Freedom allows you to select which websites you want to block, and on which of your devices.\n\nIf you try to access a blocked site during a Freedom session, your browser will instead display a calming green screen, gently reminding you that you’ve committed to getting some work done.\n\nBLOCK APPS\n\nAnother core feature of Freedom is the ability to block distracting apps. Determine which apps distract you (like games, email, Slack…), and add them as blocked apps to a Freedom session.\n\nIf you try to open those apps during a Freedom session they’ll be shut down instantly, so your attention never has a chance to be diverted.\n\nBLOCK THE ENTIRE INTERNET\n\nSometimes it’s hard to know what distractions you need to be blocking - there are so many.\n\nWhat to do? Use Freedom’s “Block All Websites” feature to essentially shut off the internet during your work session.\n\nYou can even block everything except (whitelist) if you choose, allowing yourself access to only what you need for work (including of course, Coffitivity!)\n\n[TRY FREEDOM TODAY](https://freedom.sjv.io/XxkaOa)\n\nFreedom is free to try, and if you want to use our more powerful features, we’re including an offer code, just for Coffitivity users.
